name: Solidago

project_scope.selection_mode: All 8 canonical goldenrod species indexed with range-sensitive comparisons
project_scope.range_cautions: S. mexicana is FAIL_TARGET_ZONE comparison species; S. rugosa UNRESOLVED user-approved; do not count as target-native PASS. All 8 have species cards, but S. gigantea and juliae currently use remote image links, not local copied photos.

priority: BELOW PANICLE: lower-stem hairs, smooth waxy bloom vs fuzzy vs genuinely coarse/stiff rough
MIDSTEM LEAF: number of strong veins, actual underside hair between/along veins, serrations, wrinkles, width
BASE/HABIT: creeping rhizomes and colony vs smaller isolated rosette/clump
HEAD ARRAY: one-sided recurving wand, broad arching panicle or tight terminal cluster
FNA detailed heads and phyllaries at mm scale for difficult tall vs Canada goldenrod
Site moisture & rocky/dry soil, but never habitat alone
study_strategy.warning: S. altissima, S. canadensis and S. gigantea often overlap in height, color and leaf shape. Flower color is NOT diagnostic; giant usually has genuinely smooth lower stem; altissima vs canadensis require multiple leaf/stem/head characters.

curation_status.visual_status: Eleven installed comparative panels across seven taxa, genus anatomy teaching clues and three side-by-side lessons live; fine-scale flower head, underside, hair and pappus macros still needed. Julia's remains external-only.
curation_status.scientific_notes: Julia's corrected to wet-streams-as-well-as-grasslands, fine white tomentose stem and 3–4x elongated panicle. Range labels unchanged.
curation_status.visual_lesson_standard: 2026-10-13 green-milkweed-derived photo-first Family → Genus → Species structure, with part examples and still-missing precise macros

b070_study_strategy.warning: Goldenrod flower color is not diagnostic. Use stem pubescence, leaf venation/texture, growth form, and habitat together.

quick_split: S. gigantea — smooth/glabrous lower stem, narrow 3-nerved leaves, rhizomatous, broad arching panicle; local PASS.
S. juliae — drier-site Central/west Texas species with grayer/hairier foliage and large terminal panicle; local PASS.
S. rugosa — conspicuously wrinkled leaves and hairy stems; target-zone range HOLD.
S. mexicana — coastal marsh/dune goldenrod with thick narrow leaves; target-zone FAIL.

fast_fill_note: FAST-FILL status: canonical PASS S. gigantea now has 3 diagnostic images emphasizing flower display plus leaf/stem characters. Canonical PASS S. juliae remains source-limited because the readily found licensed guide image does not expose a clean direct photo record for installation.
look_here_first: Don't start with yellow flowers. On a flowering plant, take a PHOTO of the LOWER STEM in focus (smooth/waxy? fine-haired? coarse stiff rough?). Then inspect the UNDERSIDE of a middle leaf (3 main veins? flat vs rugose? hair between veins?). THEN determine height/plant colony, dry rocky versus wet ditch setting, and the shape of the flowering branches. A single yellow plume is almost never sufficient to name a goldenrod to species.

visual_species_quick_key.look: SMOOTH lower stem, often waxy/glaucous, narrow three-veined leaves
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: S. altissima / canadensis usually short-haired at least on portions of stem; wetter drainage/moister ditch supports gigantea
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Upper inflorescence axis can still be hairy; inspect well BELOW flower branches. Three veins alone is shared.

visual_species_quick_key.look: Tall colony goldenrod: fine SHORT hairs on much of stem; firm slightly rough leaf, often only weak upper serrations; shorter/briefer involucre distinction from Canada requires hand lens
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: S. canadensis often has more regularly toothed/relatively thinner leaves and sparser longer hairs; overlap is substantial
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Do not identify merely by plant height, late flowering or between-vein hairs. Native subspecies gilvocanescens photo cannot prove every altissima.

visual_species_quick_key.look: Tall goldenrod complex: narrow three-veined leaf, often more noticeably serrated along upper leaf edge; stem more sparingly hairy than most altissima
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: S. altissima denser shorter stem hairs/firm leaves, but overlap; compare scaled involucre and leaf teeth together
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Some regional taxonomic concepts include altissima or separate taxa differently; flag ambiguous intermediate as Solidago canadensis complex.

visual_species_quick_key.look: Smaller GRAY fuzzed perennial: gray-hairy stem, tapered spatulate/oblanceolate lower leaf with winged petiole; skinny one-sided wand-like flower array
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: S. radula notably stiff ROUGH scabrous hairs and broader lower leaves with compact terminal panicle
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Dry caliche/prairie is supporting, not a diagnostic by itself.

visual_species_quick_key.look: Genuinely ROUGH, gritty stem AND leaves from short stiff hairs, often broader bottom blades; flowering array relatively compact
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: S. nemoralis has fine pale gray fuzz and more one-sided wand instead of hard gritty roughness
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Rub gently/inspect hand lens if safe; don't key just on yellow head shape.

visual_species_quick_key.look: Evenly white SOFT-HAIRY stem and narrow, 3-nerved hairy leaves (~5–10mm), LONG NARROW inflorescence about 3–4 times its width
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: Unlike gigantea smooth/glaucous stem; not necessarily dry: occurs beside WET stream and lake margins as well as in grassland/woodland
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Use soft white stem hairs, narrow panicle and leaf together, NOT drier-site identification. Exact local stem macro still missing.

visual_species_quick_key.look: RUGOSE = ridged WRINKLED or quilted leaf surfaces with curved alternate side veins; hairy stem and branched yellow panicles
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: S. radula is rough/scabrous but not necessarily visibly puckered and wrinkled in blade structure
visual_species_quick_key.caution: Strict target-zone range UNRESOLVED, USER APPROVED learner. No PASS claims.

visual_species_quick_key.look: Coastal seep, dune/brackish marsh goldenrod with thick/fleshy narrow leaves, tall often one-sided inflorescence
visual_species_quick_key.comparison: Interior tall/rough goldenrods usually softer, three-nerved serrate leaves and inland habitats
visual_species_quick_key.caution: STRICT range FAIL_TARGET_ZONE (native coastal comparison only). Do not present as confirmed Hays wild native.

visual_comparison.annotation_policy: All installed panels are unannotated study photographs. Only Giant goldenrod has a specifically role-labeled smooth-stem/underside close view in this set. Do not claim tiny phyllaries or stem-hair septation are visible in distant images; arrows remain pending individual original-pixel verification.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: SEE tiny yellow heads in branches → SPOT the lower stem and middle leaf → NAME smooth, soft-hairy, stiff-rough, wrinkled, and three-nerved → COMPARE the eight species. Never ID a goldenrod by yellow plume alone.

part_examples.title: 1 · SEE the full goldenrod plume
part_examples.look_for: At first glance this is a yellow plume. Look closer: many short branches carry many individual tiny flower HEADS (capitula). This installed Giant goldenrod photograph teaches general cluster architecture, not proof of species.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A plume is a cluster, not a single yellow flower. Begin with the big picture before inspecting parts.

part_examples.title: 2 · SPOT a smooth lower stem
part_examples.look_for: Find the comparatively SMOOTH green stem in this installed S. gigantea close view. Look beneath the flower branches, not at the hairy upper inflorescence stalk.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The lower stem distinguishes Giant from many hairy Tall/Canada goldenrods more usefully than flower color. Verify with several nodes.

part_examples.title: 3 · NAME a middle leaf's veins
part_examples.look_for: Find the middle stem leaf and its broad blade with lengthwise major veins. Three nerves are shared in the tall goldenrod complex; a better same-scale underside macro remains needed.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Leaf veins, attachment, edges and surface texture are reusable characters across goldenrods.

part_examples.title: 4 · COMPARE tall goldenrod habit
part_examples.role: flowering stem / tall goldenrod field habit
part_examples.look_for: This is an exact-taxon existing field view, NOT a verified lower-stem hair macro. Later pair same-mm close-ups of Tall vs Canada goldenrod stems and middle leaves.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Shows the overall look but keeps ID conservative where S. altissima and S. canadensis overlap.

part_examples.title: 5 · COMPARE Canada goldenrod habit
part_examples.look_for: Texas same-taxon comparison reference. Study cluster outline and find the leaf zone to photograph next; this whole-plant image alone cannot resolve the Tall/Canada complex.
part_examples.why_it_matters: A Texas reference is useful for general habit, while hair and midleaf close-ups provide the tie-breakers.

part_examples.title: 6 · Study gray goldenrod's wand
part_examples.look_for: Observe the overall inflorescence arrangement and pale gray appearance as an invitation to inspect actual fine soft stem hairs. The installed face photo is provisional; macro still needed.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Prevents confusion with rough goldenrod based only on shared yellow color or dry habitat.

part_examples.title: 7 · Compare rough goldenrod habit
part_examples.look_for: Look at the real field habit. The defining stiff GRITTY stem and leaf hairs need a close-up; don't assume these are resolved in a distant face photo.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The gray-versus-rough distinction is mainly about hair type rather than flowering shape.

part_examples.title: 8 · NEED PHOTO — one capitulum and phyllaries
part_examples.look_for: Find one individual tiny flower head (CAPITULUM), then photograph its side to reveal overlapping green PHYLLARIES (involucre), yellow ray florets, and center disk florets with a 1 mm ruler.
part_examples.why_it_matters: The best fine Goldenrod comparisons rely on real head dimensions and bracts. No verified macro is installed yet.

part_examples.title: 9 · NEED PHOTO — cypsela and pappus
part_examples.look_for: Photograph a ripe, single one-seeded CYPSELA and the hairlike PAPPUS attached to it. Use 1 mm scale; a seed-dispersal view should show the actual parts.
part_examples.why_it_matters: Completes the Asteraceae life-cycle lesson and reveals reproductive anatomy beyond pretty flowers.

learner_glossary.glaucous: GLAW-kus — dull bluish or whitish waxy bloom on a stem
learner_glossary.scabrous: SKAY-brus — coarse, rough to touch from short stiff hairs
learner_glossary.canescent: kuh-NES-ent — looks gray/whitish because of dense fine hairs
learner_glossary.triplinerved: trip-lee-NERV'D — 3 major veins, middle one plus pair running up sides from near leaf base
learner_glossary.phyllary: FILL-uh-ree — a single bract of the green cup at base of goldenrod composite flower head
learner_glossary.secund: SEE-kund — heads mostly point to one side of an axis
learner_glossary.rhizome: RY-zohm — underground spreading stem that makes new shoots

genus_diagnostics.inflorescence: The goldenrod 'plume' is made of many tiny composite FLOWER HEADS (capitula) arranged along branches. Notice whether the branches arch, form a one-sided wand, or stand in a narrower upright panicle. Flower shape is supporting evidence, not a species ID by itself.
genus_diagnostics.leaves: Inspect a MIDDLE STEM leaf from its upper surface and underside. Look for usually alternate, undivided blades; vein pattern (often three major longitudinal veins in the tall-goldenrod group), toothed versus entire margin, fine hair versus rigid roughness, and puckering (RUGOSE). Three veins do not alone prove species.
genus_diagnostics.stem: Photograph the LOWER living stem away from the flower branches, with a millimeter ruler or magnifier. Giant goldenrod is often smooth/glaucous here; Tall and Canada goldenrod may have hairs; gray goldenrod has fine gray fuzz, rough goldenrod gritty stiff hairs, and Julia's soft white hairs. Compare several stems because hairs overlap.
genus_diagnostics.flower_heads: One 'yellow flower' in Solidago is a tiny CAPITULUM containing several tubular disk florets and yellow strap-shaped ray florets. Photograph the side and face of an individual head at 1 mm scale; these details are still missing from the installed photo set.
genus_diagnostics.phyllaries: Turn a single head sideways and look for narrow overlapping green bracts called PHYLLARIES forming the INVOLUCRE. Head size, phyllary shape and tip can help difficult species, but no existing image has been certified as a measured macro. Until then this lesson is a PHOTO REQUEST, not evidence that a pictured plume shows those parts.
genus_diagnostics.fruit: Each fertilized floret matures one little dry fruit (CYPSELA) often tipped by hairlike PAPPUS bristles. Need a correctly verified Solidago mature-head macro showing one actual cypsela and its pappus; a yellow-flower habit shot does not teach this structure.
